extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology; creative writers studying narrative time
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and describing how narrative time is ordered and manipulated (anachronies, retroversions, anticipations) in fiction, including classifications, functions, and effects on reader understanding. Provides conceptual tools and heuristics for mapping story-time vs fabula-time, measuring distance/span, and deciding analytical choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning indicates what story will be about
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning of a story conventionally indicates what the story will be about (e.g., the Iliad's opening presents the grudge of Achilles and a summary of the book’s contents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the opening to present the subject and to give the reader a summary or promise that the text will fulfill (the muse’s song = what reader will hear). This helps frame subsequent anachronies and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping chronological manipulation with labeled units
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the fragment into chronological parts and indicate the order presented vs chrono­logical positions (e.g., label parts A, B, C... and record their fabula positions as numbers to show anachronies with formulas like A4-B5-C3-D2-E1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit mapping (letters for narrative presentation order; numbers for chronological/fabula order) clarifies the pattern of retroversions and anticipations and enables formal representation of anachrony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish story-time (present of narration) from fabula-time (chronological sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the primary time (the moment in the development of the fabula with which the story is concerned at the time the anachrony interrupts) and distinguish it from chronologically earlier/later fabula events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deciding the primary time is relative and analytic; pick the primary time that best accounts for the greatest number of narrative phenomena (pragmatic heuristic rather than absolute rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective vs objective anachrony
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective anachrony: an anachrony that exists only because its contents are in the past/future in the consciousness of a character (the moment of thinking is different from the events). Objective anachrony: chronologically measurable deviations not dependent on consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to separate anachronies that emulate perception/memory (subjective) from those that are narrated by the discourse at large (objective). Stream-of-consciousness texts may demand special treatment since they reproduce contents of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of anachrony relative to narrative levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Anachronies can be of different degrees depending on narrative embedding (e.g., a retroversion contained in reported speech may be a second-degree retroversion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for narrative levels when labeling anachronies (direct speech about a past event is a retroversion in the speech-level timeline and may be second-degree with respect to the primary narrative level).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological homonymy / ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is impossible to determine which fabula period a reference refers to (e.g., confusion between periods in different locations), treat the deviation as chronologically ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ambiguity is irresolvable, acknowledge it (label as achrony if necessary) rather than forcing a dubious classification; such ambiguity can be intentionally used for effects like confusion, humour, or absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance classification: external, internal, mixed anachronies
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify retroversions and anticipations by their distance from the primary fabula-time: external (completely outside primary time span), internal (occurs within primary time span), mixed (begins outside and ends within).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same threefold distinction to anticipations. Choosing the primary time span affects whether instances are internal or external; choose the solution that best accounts for the most phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of external retroversions
rubrics_metrics.description: External retroversions generally provide indications about antecedents or the past of actors insofar as that past is relevant for interpreting events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use external retroversions to supply background, antecedents, or motivating history necessary for understanding current events (e.g., antecedents that illuminate character motivations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of internal retroversions
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal retroversions often overlap with the primary fabula or fill gaps (compensate for ellipses), may provide sidetracks or new information about actors, or serve as repetition that changes the meaning of a previously described event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal retroversions can (1) fill chronological or informational gaps, (2) elaborate on already given info to change its meaning, or (3) act as a sidetrack to introduce newly relevant details. Use as structural device in detective/mystery fiction and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Span: punctual vs durative anachrony
rubrics_metrics.description: Span indicates how long the anachrony covers. Punctual anachrony evokes a single instant (punctual/preterite), durative anachrony covers a longer period (imperfect/progressive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether a retroversion/anticipation is punctual (one brief significant event) or durative (extended timeframe). This affects interpretation: punctual often highlights significance; durative sketches situation or temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete vs incomplete anachrony
rubrics_metrics.description: An anachrony is complete when the entire development from its starting point to its conclusion is presented; incomplete when it gives disconnected information or is interrupted before full development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detective and mystery narratives often use incomplete retroversions. Beginning in medias res commonly leads to complete retroversions that cover the prior events in full; interpret purpose (economy, suspense, omission) accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between span and completeness (and style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctual anachronies often recall brief but significant events and justify their interruption; durative anachronies tend to make narratives seem a succession of inevitable situations. Frequent punctual anachrony creates a bare, informative style; durative dominance gives sense of uneventful continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinations of punctual and durative anachronies to shape narrative tone and perceived causality; e.g., Proust moves between punctual openings and durative development to create expansive memory-work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipations: forms and narrative effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipations (flashforwards or opening summaries) may present outcomes in advance and can suggest fatalism/predestination or generate other types of tension by prompting questions like 'How could it have happened like this?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipations can reduce suspense about 'what' happens but replace it with tension about 'how' or 'why'. Use anticipations (including opening summaries) to control tone (fatalistic vs investigative) and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Announcements versus hints (explicit vs implicit anticipations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcements explicitly draw attention to a future event (e.g., adverbs like 'later', verbs like 'expect'), working against suspense. Hints are implicit germinal details that only reveal their anticipatory force later, increasing suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For mysteries, favour hints to sustain reader curiosity and permit a game between story and reader; for other effects, explicit announcements may be used deliberately. False hints (red herrings) can mislead readers without breaking plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: An iterative anticipation presents an event as the first of a recurring series (e.g., 'a spectacle that would weigh on our spirits every Friday from now on').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterativity signals future recurrence; however too much detailed description of the 'first occurrence' undermines its iterativity (detail makes repetition less plausible). Useful to render the first-time vantage point and foreshadow routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective retroversions increase explanatory power for subjective states
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective retroversions (memories, internal reflections) are particularly effective at explaining subjective states such as dissatisfaction or nervousness because they emulate consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the aim is psychological or political explanation (e.g., showing colonial perspectives), use subjective retroversions to ground emotions and motivations in remembered experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream-of-consciousness exception to chronological analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Stream-of-consciousness literature limits itself to reproducing contents of consciousness and is not subject to chronological analysis in the same way as other narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the methodological limitation: for pure streams of consciousness, chronological mapping tools may be inappropriate; instead focus on interior temporality and associative logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded / intertwined anachronies may be insoluble
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes anachronies are embedded in each other so tightly (e.g., retroversions inside retrospections) that analytical disentanglement is too difficult or impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases, use rough indications of time-units and study interesting fragments in detail rather than attempting an exhaustive chronological reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achrony: label for unanalysable temporal deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a temporal deviation cannot be analysed further (insufficient information or irresolvable ambiguity), designate it an achrony — a deviation of time that resists further classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the achrony label where classification would be arbitrary; treating such passages as achronies may be more analytically honest and can highlight purposeful ambiguity.
